newsitem.title: UK: British firms see women as sound investment.
newsitem.headline: British firms see women as sound investment.

text.p: Many top British companies see employing women in management as a sound business investment, the chairwoman of an equal opportunity group said on Monday.
Lady Elspeth Howe, Chairwoman of Opportunity 2000, told a news conference marking its fifth anniversary that women were a good investment.
"It is the organisations themselves who say their main reason for membership (of Opportunity 2000) is to obtain the best return on their investment," Howe said.
Opportunity 2000 is a business-led campaign which was established in 1991 to improve the quantity and quality of women's employment at all levels and in all sectors.
Business leaders who support the campaign stressed that improving equal opportunities in the workplace was more than just a women's issue and all sides stood to gain from the initiative.

Member companies, representing around 25 percent of Britain's workforce, have already introduced "family friendly" initiatives, such as flexible work schemes, enhanced maternity/paternity arrangements, career breaks and increased childcare facilities, which benefit staff.
The group estimates women will make up around 65 percent of new employees by the year 2000, and 51 percent of any organisation's workforce.
"There has been a signinficant shift in attitudes and values over the last 12 months, with more senior managers demonstrating full commitment to the campaign," said Howe.
But despite a change in company culture, Opportunity 2000 said women appointed to boardroom posts dropped to 11 percent (within Opportunity 2000 members) in 1996 from 16 percent last year.

Lord Christopher Tugendhat, chairman of bank and mortgage lender Abbey National Plc, said he felt the so-called "glass ceiling" was not the problem it used to be. As more women move up the management structure attitudes will change and so the glass ceiling will disappear he said.
"It is from the percentage of women at management level now that future chief executives will come, and this area is therefore perhaps more important," Tugendhat said.
He believed the growing numbers of women in the workforce would filter through naturally into boardroom numbers over the next five to ten years.
